That Ancus Marcius, Numa's daughter's son,
Who, after great Hostilius, here was king;
Of the same house Publius and Quintus were,
That our best water brought by conduits hither;
And [Censorinus,] nobly named so,
Twice being [by the people chosen] censor,
Was his great ancestor.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: One thus descended,
That hath beside well in his person wrought
To be set high in place, we did commend
To your remembrances: but you have found,
Scaling his present bearing with his past,
That he's your fixed enemy, and revoke
Your sudden approbation.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Say, you ne'er had done 't—
Harp on that still—but by our putting on:

And presently, when you have drawn your
number,
Repair to the Capitol.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: We will so: almost all
Repent in their election. Exeunt Citizens.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Let them go on;
This mutiny were better put in hazard,
Than stay, past doubt, for greater:
If, as his nature is, he fall in rage
With their refusal, both observe and answer
The vantage of his anger.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: To the Capitol, come:
We will be there before the stream o' the people;
And this shall seem, as partly 'tis, their own,
Which we have goaded onward. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE I
div.stage:
Cornets. Enter CORIOLANUS, MENENIUS, all
the Gentry, COMINIUS, TITUS LARTIUS, and
other Senators.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
Tullus Aufidius then had made new
head?

sp.speaker: Lart.
sp.l:
He had, my lord; and that it was
which caused
Our swifter composition.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
So then the Volsces stand but as at
first,

Ready, when time shall prompt them, to make
road
Upon's again.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: They are worn, lord consul, so,
That we shall hardly in our ages see
Their banners wave again.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Saw you Aufidius?

sp.speaker: Lart.
sp.l:
On safe-guard he came to me; and
did curse
Against the Volsces, for they had so vilely
Yielded the town: he is retired to Antium.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Spoke he of me?

sp.speaker: Lart.
sp.l: He did, my lord.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: How? what?

sp.speaker: Lart.
sp.l:
How often he had met you, sword to
sword;
That of all things upon the earth he hated

Your person most, that he would pawn his
fortunes
To hopeless restitution, so he might
Be call'd your vanquisher.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: At Antium lives he?

sp.speaker: Lart.
sp.l: At Antium.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: I wish I had a cause to seek him there,

To oppose his hatred fully. Welcome home.
Enter SICINIUS and BRUTUS.
Behold, these are the tribunes of the people,

The tongues o' the common mouth: I do despise
them;
For they do prank them in authority,
Against all noble sufferance.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Pass no further.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Ha! what is that?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: It will be dangerous to go on: no further.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: What makes this change?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: The matter?

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l:
Hath he not pass'd the noble and the
common?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Cominius, no.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Have I had children's voices?

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.l:
Tribunes, give way; he shall to
the market-place.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: The people are incensed against him.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Stop,
Or all will fall in broil.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Are these your herd?
Must these have voices, that can yield them now

And straight disclaim their tongues? What are
your offices?

You being their mouths, why rule you not their
teeth?
Have you not set them on?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Be calm, be calm.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: It is a purposed thing, and grows by plot,
To curb the will of the nobility:
Suffer 't, and live with such as cannot rule
Nor ever will be ruled.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Call't not a plot:
The people cry you mock'd them, and of late,
When corn was given them gratis, you repined;

Scandal'd the suppliants for the people, call'd
them
Time-pleasers, flatterers, foes to nobleness.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Why, this was known before.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Not to them all.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Have you inform'd them sithence?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: How! I inform them!

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: You are like to do such business.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Not unlike,
Each way, to better yours.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
Why then should I be consul? By yond
clouds,
Let me deserve so ill as you, and make me
Your fellow tribune.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: You show too much of that
For which the people stir: if you will pass

To where you are bound, you must inquire your
way,
Which you are out of, with a gentler spirit,
Or never be so noble as a consul,
Nor yoke with him for tribune.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Let's be calm.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l:
The people are abused; set on. This
paltering
Becomes not Rome, nor has Coriolanus
Deserved this so dishonour'd rub, laid falsely
I' the plain way of his merit.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Tell me of corn
This was my speech, and I will speak 't again—

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Not now, not now.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.l: Not in this heat, sir, now.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Now, as I live, I will. My nobler friends,
I crave their pardons:
For the mutable, rank-scented many, let them
Regard me as I do not flatter, and
Therein behold themselves: I say again,
In soothing them, we nourish 'gainst our senate
The cockle of rebellion, insolence, sedition,

Which we ourselves have plough'd for, sow'd, and
scatter'd,
By mingling them with us, the honour'd number,
Who lack not virtue, no, nor power, but that
Which they have given to beggars.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Well, no more.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.l: No more words, we beseech you.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: How! no more!
As for my country I have shed my blood,
Not fearing outward force, so shall my lungs
Coin words till their decay against those measles,
Which we disdain should tetter us, yet sought
The very way to catch them.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: You speak o' the people,
As if you were a god to punish, not
A man of their infirmity.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: 'Twere well
We let the people know't.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: What, what? his choler?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Choler!
Were I as patient as the midnight sleep,
By Jove! 'twould be my mind!

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: It is a mind
That shall remain a poison where it is,
Not poison any further.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Shall remain!
Hear you this Triton of the minnows? mark you
His absolute 'shall'?

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: 'Twas from the canon.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: 'Shall'!
O good but most unwise patricians! why,
You grave but reckless senators, have you thus
Given Hydra here to choose an officer,
That with his peremptory 'shall,' being but

The horn and noise o' the monster's, wants not
spirit
To say he'll turn your current in a ditch,
And make your channel his? If he have power,
Then vail your ignorance; if none, awake
Your dangerous lenity. If you are learn'd,
Be not as common fools; if you are not,

Let them have cushions by you. You are
plebeians,
If they be senators: and they are no less,

When, both your voices blended, the great'st
taste

Most palates theirs. They choose their
magistrate,
And such a one as he, who puts his 'shall,'
His popular 'shall,' against a graver bench
Than ever frown'd in Greece. By Jove himself!
It makes the consuls base: and my soul aches
To know, when two authorities are up,
Neither supreme, how soon confusion
May enter 'twixt the gap of both and take
The one by the other.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Well, on to the market-place.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Whoever gave that counsel, to give forth
The corn o' the storehouse gratis, as 'twas used
Sometime in Greece,—

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Well, well, no more of that.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
Though there the people had more
absolute power,
I say, they nourish'd disobedience, fed
The ruin of the state.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Why, shall the people give
One that speaks thus their voice?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: I'll give my reasons,

More worthier than their voices. They know the
corn
Was not our recompense, resting well assured

They ne'er did service for't: being press'd to the
war,
Even when the navel of the state was touch'd,

They would not thread the gates. This kind of
service
Did not deserve corn gratis. Being i' the war.
Their mutinies and revolts, wherein they show'd
Most valour, spoke not for them: the accusation
Which they have often made against the senate,
All cause unborn, could never be the motive
Of our so frank donation. Well, what then?
How shall this bisson multitude digest
The senate's courtesy? Let deeds express
What's like to be their words: 'We did request it;
We are the greater poll, and in true fear
They gave us our demands.' Thus we debase
The nature of our seats and make the rabble
Call our cares fears; which will in time
Break ope the locks o' the senate and bring in
The crows to peck the eagles.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Come, enough.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Enough, with over-measure.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: No, take more:
What may be sworn by, both divine and human,
Seal what I end withal! This double worship,

Where one part does disdain with cause, the
other

Insult without all reason, where gentry, title,
wisdom,
Cannot conclude but by the yea and no
Of general ignorance,—it must omit
Real necessities, and give way the while

To unstable slightness: purpose so barr'd, it
follows,

Nothing is done to purpose. Therefore, beseech
you,—
You that will be less fearful than discreet,
That love the fundamental part of state
More than you doubt the change on't, that prefer
A noble life before a long, and wish
To jump a body with a dangerous physic
That's sure of death without it, at once pluck out
The multitudinous tongue; let them not lick
The sweet which is their poison: your dishonour
Mangles true judgement and bereaves the state
Of that integrity which should become't,
Not having the power to do the good it would,
For the ill which doth control't.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Has said enough.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Has spoken like a traitor, and shall answer
As traitors do.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Thou wretch, despite o'erwhelm thee!

What should the people do with these bald
tribunes ?
On whom depending, their obedience fails
To the greater bench: in a rebellion,
When what's not meet, but what must be was law,
Then were they chosen: in a better hour,
Let what is meet be said it must be meet,
And throw their power i' the dust.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Manifest treason!

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: This a consul? no.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l:
The ædiles, ho!
Enter an Ædile.
Let him be apprehended,

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l:
Go, call the people: Exit Ædile in
whose name myself
Attach thee as a traitorous innovator,
A foe to the public weal: obey, I charge thee,
And follow to thine answer.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Hence, old goat!

sp.speaker: Senators, &c.
sp.l: We'll surety him.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Aged sir, hands off.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
Hence, rotten thing! or I shall shake
thy bones
Out of thy garments.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l:
Help, ye citizens!
Enter a rabble of Citizens (Plebeians), with the
Ædiles.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: On both sides more respect.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l:
Here's he that would take from you all
your power.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Seize him, ædiles!

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l: Down with him! down with him!

sp.speaker: Senators, &c.
sp.l:
Weapons, weapons, weapons!
They all bustle about Coriolanus, crying

'Tribunes!' 'Patricians!' 'Citizens!' 'What,
ho!'
'Sicinius!' 'Brutus!' 'Coriolanus!' 'Citizens!'
'Peace, peace, peace!' 'Stay, hold, peace!'

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
What is about to be? I am out of
breath;
Confusion's near; I cannot speak. You, tribunes
To the people! Coriolanus, patience!
Speak, good Sicinius.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Hear me, people; peace!

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l:
Let's hear our tribune: peace!
Speak; speak, speak.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: You are at point to lose your liberties:
Marcius would have all from you; Marcius,
Whom late you have named for consul.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Fie, fie, fie!
This is the way to kindle, not to quench.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.l:
To unbuild the city and to lay all
flat.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: What is the city but the people?

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l: True,
The people are the city.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: By the consent of all, we were establish'd
The people's magistrates.

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l: You so remain.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: And so are like to do.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: That is the way to lay the city flat;
To bring the roof to the foundation,
And bury all, which yet distinctly ranges,
In heaps and piles of ruin.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: This deserves death.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Or let us stand to our authority,
Or let us lose it. We do here pronounce,
Upon the part o' the people, in whose power
We were elected theirs, Marcius is worthy
Of present death.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Therefore lay hold of him;
Bear him to the rock Tarpeian, and from thence
Into destruction cast him.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Ædiles, seize him!

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l: Yield, Marcius, yield!

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Hear me one word;
Beseech you, tribunes, hear me but a word.

sp.speaker: Æd.
sp.l: Peace, peace!

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
Be that you seem, truly
your country's friend,
And temperately proceed to what you would
Thus violently redress.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Sir, those cold ways,
That seem like prudent helps, are very poisonous

Where the disease is violent. Lay hands upon
him,
And bear him to the rock.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
No, I'll die here.
Drawing his sword.
There's some among you have beheld me fighting:
Come, try upon yourselves what you have seen me.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
Down with that sword! Tribunes,
withdraw awhile.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Lay hands upon him.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Help Marcius, help,
You that be noble; help him, young and old!

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l:
Down with him, down with himl
In this mutiny, the Tribunes, the Ædiles,
and the People, are beat in.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
Go, get you to your house; be gone,
away!
All will be naught else.

sp.speaker: Sec. Sen.
sp.l: Get you gone.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Stand fast;
We have as many friends as enemies.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Shall it be put to that?

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.l: The gods forbid!
I prithee, noble friend, home to thy house;
Leave us to cure this cause.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: For 'tis a sore upon us,
You cannot tent yourself: be gone, beseech you.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Come, sir, along with us.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
I would they were barbarians—as they
are,

Though in Rome litter'd—not Romans—as they
are not,
Though calved i' the porch o' the Capitol—

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Be gone;
Put not your worthy rage into your tongue;
One time will owe another.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: On fair ground
I could beat forty of them.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: I could myself

Take up a brace o' the best of them; yea, the
two tribunes.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: But now 'tis odds beyond arithmetic;
And manhood is call'd foolery, when it stands
Against a falling fabric. Will you hence,
Before the tag return? whose rage doth rend
Like interrupted waters and o'erbear
What they are used to bear.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Pray you, be gone:
I'll try whether my old wit be in request

With those that have but little: this must be
patch'd
With cloth of any colour.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l:
Nay, come away.
Exeunt Coriolanus, Cominius, and others.

sp.speaker: A Patrician.
sp.l: This man has marr'd his fortune.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: His nature is too noble for the world:
He would not flatter Neptune for his trident,

Or Jove for's power to thunder. His heart's his
mouth:
What his breast forges, that his tongue must vent;
And, being angry, does forget that ever
He heard the name of death.A noise within.
Here's goodly work!

sp.speaker: Sec. Pat.
sp.l: I would they were a-bed!

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
I would they were in Tiber! What the
vengeance!

Could he not speak 'em fair?
Re-enter BRUTUS and SICINIUS, with the rabble.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Where is this viper
That would depopulate the city and
Be every man himself?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: You worthy tribunes,—

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l:
He shall be thrown down the Tarpeian
rock
With rigorous hands: he hath resisted law,
And therefore law shall scorn him further trial
Than the severity of the public power
Which he so sets at nought.

sp.speaker: First Cit.
sp.l: He shall well know
The noble tribunes are the people's mouths,
And we their hands.

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l: He shall, sure on't.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Sir, sir,—

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Peace!

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
Do not cry havoc, where you should but
hunt
With modest warrant.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Sir, how comes't that you
Have holp to make this rescue?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Hear me speak:
As I do know the consul's worthiness,
So can I name his faults,—

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Consul! what consul?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: The consul Coriolanus.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: He consul!

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l: No, no, no, no, no.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
If, by the tribunes' leave, and yours,
good people,
I may be heard, I would crave a word or two;
The which shall turn you to no further harm
Than so much loss of time.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Speak briefly then;
For we are peremptory to dispatch
This viperous traitor: to eject him hence
Were but one danger, and to keep him here
Our certain death: therefore it is decreed
He dies to-night.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Now the good gods forbid
That our renowned Rome, whose gratitude
Towards her deserved children is enroll'd
In Jove's own book, like an unnatural dam
Should now eat up her own!

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: He's a disease that must be cut away.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: O, he's a limb that has but a disease;
Mortal, to cut it off; to cure it, easy.
What has he done to Rome that's worthy death?
Killing our enemies, the blood he hath lost—
Which, I dare vouch, is more than that he hath,
By many an ounce—he dropp'd it for his country;
And what is left, to lose it by his country,
Were to us all, that do't and suffer it,
A brand to the end o' the world.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: This is clean kam.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l:
Merely awry: when he did love his
country,
It honour'd him.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: The service of the foot
Being once gangrened, is not then respected
For what before it was.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: We'll hear no more.
Pursue him to his house, and pluck him thence;
Lest his infection, being of catching nature,
Spread further.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: One word more, one word.
This tiger-footed rage, when it shall find
The harm of unscann'd swiftness, will too late

Tie leaden pounds to's heels. Proceed by
process;
Lest parties, as he is beloved, break out,
And sack great Rome with Romans.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: If it were so,—

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: What do ye talk?
Have we not had a taste of his obedience?
Our ædiles smote? ourselves resisted? Come.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
Consider this: he has been bred i' the
wars
Since he could draw a sword, and is ill school'd
In bolted language; meal and bran together
He throws without distinction. Give me leave,
I'll go to him, and undertake to bring him
Where he shall answer, by a lawful form,
In peace, to his utmost peril.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.l: Noble tribunes,
It is the humane way: the other course
Will prove too bloody, and the end of it
Unknown to the beginning.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Noble Menenius,
Be you then as the people's officer.
Masters, lay down your weapons.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Go not home.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l:
Meet on the market-place. We'll attend
you there:
Where, if you bring not Marcius, we'll proceed
In our first way,

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: I'll bring him to you. To the Senators

Let me desire your company:
he must come,
Or what is worst will follow.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.l: Pray you, let's to him. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
Let them pull all about mine ears,
present me
Death on the wheel or at wild horses' heels,
Or pile ten hills on the Tarpeian rock,
That the precipitation might down stretch
Below the beam of sight, yet will I still
Be thus to them.

sp.speaker: A Patrician.
sp.l: You do the nobler.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: I muse my mother
Does not approve me further, who was wont
To call them woollen vassals, things created
To buy and sell with groats, to show bare heads
In congregations, to yawn, be still and wonder,
When one but of my ordinance stood up

To speak of peace or war.
Enter VOLUMNIA.
I talk of you:

Why did you wish me milder? would you
have me
False to my nature? Rather say I play
The man I am.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l: O, sir, sir, sir,
I would have had you put your power well on,
Before you had worn it out.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Let go.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l:
You might have been enough the man
you are,
With striving less to be so: lesser had been
The thwartings of your dispositions, if
You had not show'd them how ye were disposed
Ere they lack'd power to cross you.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Let them hang.

sp.speaker: A Patrician.
sp.l:
Ay, and burn too.
Enter MENENIUS and Senators.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
Come, come, you have been too rough,
something too rough;
You must return and mend it.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.l: There's no remedy;
Unless, by not so doing, our good city
Cleave in the midst, and perish.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l: Pray, be counsell'd:
I have a heart as little apt as yours,
But yet a brain that leads my use of anger
To better vantage.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Well said, noble woman!
Before he should thus stoop to the herd, but that
The violent fit o' the time craves it as physic
For the whole state, I would put mine armour on.
Which I can scarcely bear.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: What must I do?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Return to the tribunes.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Well, what then? what then?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Repent what you have spoke.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: For them! I cannot do it to the gods;
Must I then do't to them?

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l: You are too absolute;
Though therein you can never be too noble,

But when extremities speak. I have heard
you say,
Honour and policy, like unsever'd friends,

I' the war do grow together: grant that, and
tell me,
In peace what each of them by the other lose,
That they combine not there.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Tush, tush!

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: A good demand.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l: If it be honour in your wars to seem
The same you are not, which, for your best ends,
You adopt your policy, how is it less or worse,
That it shall hold companionship in peace
With honour, as in war, since that to both
It stands in like request?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Why force you this?

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l:
Because that now it lies you on to
speak
To the people; not by your own instruction,
Nor by the matter which your heart prompts you,
But with such words that are but roted in
Your tongue, though but bastards and syllables
Of no allowance to your bosom's truth.
Now, this no more dishonours you at all
Than to take in a town with gentle words,
Which else would put you to your fortune and
The hazard of much blood.
I would dissemble with my nature where
My fortunes and my friends at stake required
I should do so in honour: I am in this,
Your wife, your son, these senators, the nobles;
And you will rather show our general louts
How you can frown than spend a fawn upon 'em,
For the inheritance of their loves and safeguard
Of what that want might ruin.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Noble lady!
Come, go with us; speak fair: you may salve so,
Not what is dangerous present, but the loss
Of what is past.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l: I prithee now, my son,
Go to them, with this bonnet in thy hand;

And thus far having stretch'd it—here be with
them—
Thy knee bussing the stones—for in such business
Action is eloquence, and the eyes of the ignorant
More learned than the ears—waving thy head,
Which often, thus, correcting thy stout heart,
Now humble as the ripest mulberry
That will not hold the handling: or say to them,
Thou art their soldier, and being bred in broils
Hast not the soft way which, thou dost confess,
Were fit for thee to use as they to claim,
In asking their good loves, but thou wilt frame
Thyself, forsooth, hereafter theirs, so far
As thou hast power and person.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: This but done,

Even as she speaks, why, their hearts were
yours;
For they have pardons, being ask'd, as free
As words to little purpose.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l: Prithee now,

Go, and be ruled: although I know thou hadst
rather
Follow thine enemy in a fiery gulf

Than flatter him in a bower. Here is Cominius.
Enter COMINIUS.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l:
I have been i' the market-place; and,
sir, 'tis fit,
You make strong party, or defend yourself
By calmness or by absence: all's in anger.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Only fair speech.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: I think 'twill serve, if he
Can thereto frame his spirit.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l: He must, and will.
Prithee now, say you will, and go about it.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
Must I go show them my unbarbed
sconce?
Must I with base tongue give my noble heart
A lie that it must bear? Well, I will do't:
Yet, were there but this single plot to lose,

This mould of Marcius, they to dust should
grind it

And throw 't against the wind. To the
marketplace!
You have put me now to such a part which never
I shall discharge to the life.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Come, come, we'll prompt you.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l:
I prithee now, sweet son, as thou hast
said
My praises made thee first a soldier, so,
To have my praise for this, perform a part
Thou hast not done before.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Well, I must do't:
Away, my disposition, and possess me
Some harlot's spirit! my throat of war be turn'd,
Which quired with my drum, into a pipe
Small as an eunuch, or the virgin voice
That babies lulls asleep! the smiles of knaves
Tent in my cheeks, and schoolboys' tears take up
The glasses of my sight! a beggar's tongue

Make motion through my lips, and my arm'd
knees,
Who bow'd but in my stirrup, bend like his
That hath received an alms! I will not do't,
Lest I surcease to honour mine own truth
And by my body's action teach my mind
A most inherent baseness.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l: At thy choice, then:
To beg of thee, it is my more dishonour
Than thou of them. Come all to ruin; let
Thy mother rather feel thy pride than fear
Thy dangerous stoutness, for I mock at death
With as big heart as thou. Do as thou list.

Thy valiantness was mine, thou suck'dst it
from me,
But owe thy pride thyself.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Pray, be content:
Mother, I am going to the market-place;
Chide me no more. I'll mountebank their loves,

Cog their hearts from them, and come home
beloved
Of all the trades in Rome. Look, I am going:
Commend me to my wife. I'll return consul;
Or never trust to what my tongue can do
I' the way of flattery further.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l: Do your will. Exit.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l:
Away! the tribunes do attend you:
arm yourself
To answer mildly; for they are prepared
With accusations, as I hear, more strong
Than are upon you yet.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
The word is 'mildly.' Pray you, let
us go:
Let them accuse me by invention, I
Will answer in mine honour.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Ay, but mildly.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Well, mildly be it then. Mildly! Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l:
In this point charge him home, that he
affects
Tyrannical power: if he evade us there,
Enforce him with his envy to the people,
And that the spoil got on the Antiates

Was ne'er distributed.
Enter an Ædile.
What, will he come?

sp.speaker: Æd.
sp.l: He's coming.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: How accompanied?

sp.speaker: Æd.
sp.l: With old Menenius, and those senators
That always favour'd him.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Have you a catalogue
Of all the voices that we have procured
Set down by the poll?

sp.speaker: Æd.
sp.l: I have; 'tis ready.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Have you collected them by tribes?

sp.speaker: Æd.
sp.l: I have.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Assemble presently the people hither;
And when they hear me say 'It shall be so

I' the right and strength o' the commons,' be it
either

For death, for fine, or banishment, then let
them,
If I say fine, cry 'Fine;' if death, cry 'Death.'
Insisting on the old prerogative
And power i' the truth o' the cause.

sp.speaker: Æd.
sp.l: I shall inform them.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l:
And when such time they have begun
to cry,
Let them not cease, but with a din confused
Enforce the present execution
Of what we chance to sentence.

sp.speaker: Æd.
sp.l: Very well.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l:
Make them be strong and ready for this
hint,
When we shall hap to give 't them.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Go about it. Exit Ædile.
Put him to choler straight: he hath been used
Ever to conquer, and to have his worth
Of contradiction: being once chafed, he cannot
Be rein'd again to temperance; then he speaks
What's in his heart; and that is there which looks
With us to break his neck.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l:
Well, here he comes.
Enter CORIOLANUS, MENENIUS, and COMINIUS,
with Senators and Patricians.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Calmly, I do beseech you.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Ay, as an ostler, that for the poorest piece

Will bear the knave by the volume. The
honour'd gods
Keep Rome in safety, and the chairs of justice
Supplied with worthy men! plant love among 's!
Throng our large temples with the shows of peace,
And not our streets with war!

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.l: Amen, amen.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
A noble wish.
Re-enter Ædile, with Citizens.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Draw near, ye people.

sp.speaker: Æd.
sp.l:
List to your tribunes. Audience! peace,
I say!

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: First, hear me speak.

sp.speaker: Both Tri.
sp.l: Well, say. Peace, ho!

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
Shall I be charged no further than this
present?
Must all determine here?

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: I do demand,
If you submit you to the people's voices,
Allow their officers and are content
To suffer lawful censure for such faults
As shall be proved upon you?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: I am content.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Lo, citizens, he says he is content:
The warlike service he has done, consider; think
Upon the wounds his body bears, which show
Like graves i' the holy churchyard.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Scratches with briers,
Scars to move laughter only.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Consider further,
That when he speaks not like a citizen,
You find him like a soldier: do not take
His rougher accents for malicious sounds,
But, as I say, such as become a soldier,
Rather than envy you.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Well, well, no more.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: What is the matter
That being pass'd for consul with full voice,
I am so dishonour'd that the very hour
You take it off again?

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Answer to us.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Say, then: 'tis true, I ought so.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l:
We charge you, that you have contrived
to take
From Rome all season'd office and to wind
Yourself into a power tyrannical;
For which you are a traitor to the people.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: How! traitor!

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Nay, temperately; your promise.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
The fires i' the lowest hell fold-in the
people!
Call me their traitor! Thou injurious tribune!
Within thine eyes sat twenty thousand deaths,
In thy hands clutch'd as many millions, in
Thy lying tongue both numbers, I would say
'Thou liest' unto thee with a voice as free
As I do pray the gods.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Mark you this, people?

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l: To the rock, to the rock with him!

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Peace!
We need not put new matter to his charge:
What you have seen him do and heard him speak,
Beating your officers, cursing yourselves,
Opposing laws with strokes and here defying

Those whose great power must try him; even
this,
So criminal and in such capital kind,
Deserves the extremest death.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: But since he hath
Served well for Rome,—

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: What do you prate of service?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: I talk of that, that know it.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: You?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
Is this the promise that you made your
mother?

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Know, I pray you,—

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: I'll know no further:
Let them pronounce the steep Tarpeian death,
Vagabond exile, flaying, pent to linger
But with a grain a day, I would not buy
Their mercy at the price of one fair word;
Nor check my courage for what they can give,
To have't with saying 'Good morrow.'

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: For that he has,
As much as in him lies, from time to time
Envied against the people, seeking means
To pluck away their power, as now at last
Given hostile strokes, and that not in the presence
Of dreaded justice, but on the ministers
That do distribute it; in the name o' the people
And in the power of us the tribunes, we,
Even from this instant, banish him our city,
In peril of precipitation
From off the rock Tarpeian never more
To enter our Rome gates: i' the people's name,
I say it shall be so.

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l:
It shall be so, it shall be so; let him
away:
He 's banish'd, and it shall be so.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l:
Hear me, my masters, and my common
friends,—

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: He's sentenced; no more hearing.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Let me speak:
I have been consul, and can show for Rome
Her enemies' marks upon me. I do love
My country's good with a respect more tender,
More holy and profound, than mine own life,
My dear wife's estimate, her womb's increase,
And treasure of my loins; then if I would
Speak that,—

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: We know your drift: speak what?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l:
There's no more to be said, but he is
banish'd,
As enemy to the people and his country:
It shall be so.

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l: It shall be so, it shall be so.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
You common cry of curs! whose breath
I hate
As reek o' the rotten fens, whose loves I prize
As the dead carcasses of unburied men
That do corrupt my air, I banish you;
And here remain with your uncertainty!
Let every feeble rumour shake your hearts!
Your enemies, with nodding of their plumes,
Fan you into despair! Have the power still
To banish your defenders; till at length
Your ignorance, which finds not till it feels,
Making not reservation of yourselves,
Still your own foes, deliver you as most
Abated captives to some nation
That won you without blows! Despising,
For you, the city, thus I turn my back:

There is a world elsewhere.
Exeunt Coriolanus, Cominius,
Menenius, Senators, and Patricians.

sp.speaker: Æd.
sp.l: The people's enemy is gone, is gone!

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l:
Our enemy is banish'd! he is gone!
Hoo! hoo! Shouting, and throwing up
their caps.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Go, see him out at gates, and follow him,
As he hath follow'd you, with all despite;
Give him deserved vexation. Let a guard
Attend us through the city.

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l:
Come, come; let's see him out at
gates; come.
The gods preserve our noble tribunes! Come. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE I
div.stage: Rome. Before a gate of the city.

Enter CORIOLANUS, VOLUMNIA, VIRGILIA,
MENENIUS, COMINIUS, with the young Nobility of
Rome.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
Come, leave your tears: a brief
farewell: the beast
With many heads butts me away. Nay, mother,
Where is your ancient courage? you were used
To say extremity was the trier of spirits;
That common chances common men could bear;
That when the sea was calm all boats alike
Show'd mastership in floating; fortune's blows,

When most struck home, being gentle wounded,
craves
A noble cunning: you were used to load me
With precepts that would make invincible
The heart that conn'd them.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: O heavens! O heavens!

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Nay, I prithee, woman,—

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l:
Now the red pestilence strike all trades
in Rome,
And occupations perish!

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: What, what, what!
I shall be loved when I am lack'd. Nay, mother,
Resume that spirit, when you were wont to say,
If you had been the wife of Hercules,
Six of his labours you 'ld have done, and saved
Your husband so much sweat. Cominius,
Droop not; adieu. Farewell, my wife, my mother:
I'll do well yet. Thou old and true Menenius,
Thy tears are salter than a younger man's,

And venomous to thine eyes. My sometime
general,
I have seen thee stern, and thou hast oft beheld
Heart-hardening spectacles; tell these sad women
'Tis fond to wail inevitable strokes,
As 'tis to laugh at 'em. My mother, you wot well
My hazards still have been your solace: and
Believe 't not lightly—though I go alone,
Like to a lonely dragon, that his fen

Makes fear'd and talk'd of more than seen—your
son
Will or exceed the common or be caught
With cautelous baits and practice.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l: My first son,
Whither wilt thou go? Take good Cominius
With thee awhile: determine on some course,
More than a wild exposture to each chance
That starts i' the way before thee.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: O the gods!

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l:
I'll follow thee a month, devise with
thee
Where thou shalt rest, that thou mayst hear of us
And we of thee: so if the time thrust forth
A cause for thy repeal, we shall not send
O'er the vast world to seek a single man,
And lose advantage, which doth ever cool
I' the absence of the needer.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Fare ye well:
Thou hast years upon thee; and thou art too full
Of the wars' surfeits, to go rove with one
That's yet unbruised: bring me but out at gate.
Come, my sweet wife, my dearest mother, and
My friends of noble touch, when I am forth,
Bid me farewell, and smile. I pray you, come.
While I remain above the ground, you shall
Hear from me still, and never of me aught
But what is like me formerly.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: That's worthily
As any ear can hear. Come, let's not weep.
If I could shake off but one seven years
From these old arms and legs, by the good gods,
I'ld with thee every foot.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Give me thy hand:
Come. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE II
div.stage: The same. A street near the gate.
Enter SICINIUS, BRUTUS, and an Ædile.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l:
Bid them all home; he's gone, and we'll
no further.
The nobility are vex'd, whom we see have sided
In his behalf.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Now we have shown our power,
Let us seem humbler after it is done
Than when it was a-doing.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Bid them home:
Say their great enemy is gone, and they
Stand in their ancient strength.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Dismiss them home. Exit Ædile.
Here comes his mother.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Let's not meet her.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: They say she's mad.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l:
They have ta'en note of us: keep on
your way.
Enter VOLUMNIA, VIRGILIA, and MENENIUS.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l:
O, ye're well met: the hoarded plague
o' the gods
Requite your love!

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Peace, peace; be not so loud.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l:
If that I could for weeping, you should
hear,—
Nay, and you shall hear some. To Brutus
Will you be gone?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l:
You shall stay too: I
would I had the power
To say so to my husband.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Are you mankind?

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l:
Ay, fool; is that a shame? Note but
this fool.
Was not a man my father? Hadst thou foxship
To banish him that struck more blows for Rome
Than thou hast spoken words?

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: O blessed heavens!

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l:
More noble blows than ever thou wise
words;

And for Rome's good. I'll tell thee what;
yet go:
Nay, but thou shalt stay too: I would my son
Were in Arabia, and thy tribe before him,
His good sword in his hand.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: What then?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: What then!
He'ld make an end of thy posterity.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l: Bastards and all.

Good man, the wounds that he does bear for
Rome!

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Come, come, peace.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: I would he had continued to his country
As he began, and not unknit himself
The noble knot he made.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: I would he had.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l:
'I would he had'! 'Twas you incensed
the rabble:
Cats, that can judge as fitly of his worth
As I can of those mysteries which heaven
Will not have earth to know.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Pray, let us go.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l: Now, pray, sir, get you gone:

You have done a brave deed. Ere you go, hear
this:—
As far as doth the Capitol exceed
The meanest house in Rome, so far my son—
This lady's husband here, this, do you see?—
Whom you have banish'd, does exceed you all.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Well, well, we'll leave you.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Why stay we to be baited
With one that wants her wits?

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l:
Take my prayers with you.
Exeunt Tribunes.
I would the gods had nothing else to do
But to confirm my curses! Could I meet 'em
But once a-day, it would unclog my heart
Of what lies heavy to't.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: You have told them home;

And, by my troth, you have cause. You'll sup
with me?

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l: Anger's my meat; I sup upon myself.
And so shall starve with feeding. Come, let's go:
Leave this faint puling and lament as I do,
In anger, Juno-like. Come, come, come.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Fie, fie, fie! Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE III
div.stage:
A highway between Rome
and Antium.
Enter a Roman and a Volsce, meeting.

sp.speaker: Rom.
sp.p: I know you well, sir, and you know me: your name, I think, is Adrian.

sp.speaker: Vols.
sp.p: It is so, sir: truly, I have forgot you.

sp.speaker: Rom.
sp.p: I am a Roman; and my services are, as you are, against 'em: know you me yet?

sp.speaker: Vols.
sp.p: Nicanor? no.

sp.speaker: Rom.
sp.p: The same, sir.

sp.speaker: Vols.
sp.p: You had more beard when I last saw you; but your favour is well approved by your tongue. What's the news in Rome? I have a note from the Volscian state, to find you out there: you have well saved me a day's journey.

sp.speaker: Rom.
sp.p: There hath been in Rome strange insurrections; the people against the senators, patricians, and nobles.

sp.speaker: Vols.
sp.p: Hath been! is it ended, then? Our state thinks not so: they are in a most war-like preparation, and hope to come upon them in the heat of their division.

sp.speaker: Rom.
sp.p: The main blaze of it is past, but a small thing would make it flame again: for the nobles receive so to heart the banishment of that worthy Coriolanus, that they are in a ripe aptness to take all power from the people and to pluck from them their tribunes for ever. This lies glowing, I can tell you, and is almost mature for the violent breaking out.

sp.speaker: Vols.
sp.p: Coriolanus banished!

sp.speaker: Rom.
sp.p: Banished, sir.

sp.speaker: Vols.
sp.p: You will be welcome with this intelligence, Nicanor.

sp.speaker: Rom.
sp.p: The day serves well for them now. I have heard it said, the fittest time to corrupt a man's wife is when she's fallen out with her husband. Your noble Tullus Aufidius will appear well in these wars, his great opposer, Coriolanus, being now in no request of his country.

sp.speaker: Vols.
sp.p: He cannot choose. I am most fortunate, thus accidentally to encounter you: you have ended my business, and I will merrily accompany you home.

sp.speaker: Rom.
sp.p: I shall, between this and supper, tell you most strange things from Rome; all tending to the good of their adversaries. Have you an army ready, say you?

sp.speaker: Vols.
sp.p: A most royal one; the centurions and their charges, distinctly billeted, already in the entertainment, and to be on foot at an hour's warning.

sp.speaker: Rom.
sp.p: I am joyful to hear of their readiness, and am the man, I think, that shall set them in present action. So, sir, heartily well met, and most glad of your company.

sp.speaker: Vols.
sp.p: You take my part from me, sir; I have the most cause to be glad of yours.

sp.speaker: Rom.
sp.p: Well, let us go together. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE IV
div.stage:
Enter CORIOLANUS in mean apparel, disguised
and muffled.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: A goodly city is this Antium. City,
'Tis I that made thy widows: many an heir
Of these fair edifices 'fore my wars

Have I heard groan and drop: then know
me not,

Lest that thy wives with spits and boys with
stones

In puny battle slay me.
Enter a Citizen.
Save you, sir.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: And you.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Direct me, if it be your will,
Where great Aufidius lies; is he in Antium?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: He is, and feasts the nobles of the state
At his house this night.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Which is his house, beseech you?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: This, here before you.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
Thank you, sir: farewell.
Exit Citizen.

O world, thy slippery turns! Friends now fast
sworn,
Whose double bosoms seem to wear one heart,

Whose hours, whose bed, whose meal, and
exercise,
Are still together, who twin, as 'twere, in love
Unseparable, shall within this hour,
On a dissension of a doit, break out
To bitterest enmity: so, fellest foes,

Whose passions and whose plots have broke their
sleep
To take the one the other, by some chance,

Some trick not worth an egg, shall grow dear
friends
And interjoin their issues. So with me:
My birth-place hate I, and my love's upon
This enemy town. I'll enter: if he slay me,
He does fair justice; if he give me way,
I'll do his country service. Exit.

div.head: SCENE V
div.stage:
The same. A hall in Aufidius's
house.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p:
Wine, wine, wine! What service is here! I think our fellows are asleep. Exit.
Enter a second Servingman.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serve.
sp.p:
Where's Cotus? my master calls for him. Cotus! Exit.
Enter CORIOLANUS.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
A goodly house: the feast smells well;
but I

Appear not like a guest.
Re-enter the first Servingman.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: What would you have, friend? whence are you? Here's no place for you: pray, go to the door. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: I have deserved no better entertainment,

In being Coriolanus.
Re-enter second Servingman.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: Whence are you, sir? Has the porter his eyes in his head, that he gives entrance to such companions? Pray, get you out.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: Away!

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: Away! get you away.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: Now thou'rt troublesome.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p:
Are you so brave? I'll have you talked with anon.
Enter a third Servingman. The first meets him.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: What fellow's that?

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: A strange one as ever I looked on: I cannot get him out o' the house: prithee, call my master to him. Retires.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: What have you to do here, fellow? Pray you, avoid the house.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: Let me but stand; I will not hurt your hearth.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: What are you?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: A gentleman.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: A marvellous poor one.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: True, so I am.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: Pray you, poor gentleman, take up some other station; here's no place for you; pray you, avoid: come.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: Follow your function, go, and batten on cold bits. Pushes him awAy.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: What, you will not? Prithee, tell my master what a strange guest he has here.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: And I shall. Exit.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: Where dwellest thou?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: Under the canopy.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: Under the canopy?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: Ay.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: Where's that?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: I' the city of kites and crows.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: I' the city of kites and crows! What an ass it is! Then thou dwellest with daws too?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: No, I serve not thy master.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: How, sir! do you meddle with my master?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
Ay; 'tis an honester service than to meddle with thy mistress. Thou pratest, and pratest; serve with thy trencher,hence!
Beats him away. Exit third Servingman.
Enter AUFIDIUS with the second Servingman.

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: Where is this fellow?

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: Here, sir: I'ld have beaten him like a dog, but for disturbing the lords within. Retires.

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l:
Whence comest thou? what wouldst
thou? thy name?
Why speak'st not? speak, man: what's thy name?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: If, Tullus, Unmuffling.

Not yet thou knowest me, and, seeing me,
dost not
Think me for the man I am, necessity
Commands me name myself.

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: What is thy name?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: A name unmusical to the Volscians' ears,
And harsh in sound to thine.

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: Say, what's thy name?
Thou hast a grim appearance, and thy face
Bears a command in't; though thy tackle's torn,
Thou show'st a noble vessel: what's thy name ?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
Prepare thy brow to frown: know'st
thou me yet?

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: I know thee not: thy name?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: My name is Caius Marcius, who hath done
To thee particularly and to all the Volsces
Great hurt and mischief; thereto witness may
My surname, Coriolanus: the painful service,
The extreme dangers and the drops of blood
Shed for my thankless country are requited
But with that surname; a good memory,
And witness of the malice and displeasure

Which thou shouldst bear me: only that name
remains;
The cruelty and envy of the people,
Permitted by our dastard nobles, who
Have all forsook me, hath devour'd the rest;
And suffer'd me by the voice of slaves to be
Whoop'd out of Rome. Now this extremity
Hath brought me to thy hearth; not out of hope—
Mistake me not—to save my life, for if
I had fear'd death, of all the men i' the world
I would have 'voided thee, but in mere spite,
To be full quit of those my banishers,
Stand I before thee here. Then if thou hast
A heart of wreak in thee, that wilt revenge
Thine own particular wrongs and stop those maims

Of shame seen through thy country, speed thee
straight,
And make my misery serve thy turn: so use it
That my revengeful services may prove
As benefits to thee, for I will fight
Against my canker'd country with the spleen
Of all the under fiends. But if so be

Thou durst not this and that to prove more
fortunes
Thou 'rt tired, then, in a word, I also am
Longer to live most weary, and present
My throat to thee and to thy ancient malice;
Which not to cut would show thee but a fool,
Since I have ever follow'd thee with hate,
Drawn tuns of blood out of thy country's breast,
And cannot live but to thy shame, unless
It be to do thee service.

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: O Marcius, Marcius!

Each word thou hast spoke hath weeded from my
heart
A root of ancient envy. If Jupiter
Should from yond cloud speak divine things,
And say ‘’Tis true,’ I'ld not believe them more
Than thee, all noble Marcius. Let me twine
Mine arms about that body, where against
My grained ash an hundred times hath broke,
And scarr'd the moon with splinters: here I clip
The anvil of my sword, and do contest
As hotly and as nobly with thy love
As ever in ambitious strength I did
Contend against thy valour. Know thou first,
I loved the maid I married; never man
Sigh'd truer breath; but that I see thee here,
Thou noble thing! more dances my rapt heart
Than when I first my wedded mistress saw

Bestride my threshold. Why, thou Mars! I tell
thee,
We have a power on foot; and I had purpose
Once more to hew thy target from thy brawn,
Or lose mine arm for't: thou hast beat me out
Twelve several times, and I have nightly since
Dreamt of encounters 'twixt thyself and me:
We have been down together in my sleep,
Unbuckling helms, fisting each other's throat,

And waked half dead with nothing. Worthy
Marcius,
Had we no quarrel else to Rome, but that
Thou art thence banish'd, we would muster all
From twelve to seventy, and pouring war
Into the bowels of ungrateful Rome,
Like a bold flood o'er-bear. O, come, go in,
And take our friendly senators by the hands;
Who now are here, taking their leaves of me,
Who am prepared against your territories,
Though not for Rome itself.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: You bless me, gods!

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l:
Therefore, most absolute sir, if thou wilt
have
The leading of thine own revenge, take
The one half of my commission; and set down—
As best thou art experienced, since thou know'st

Thy country's strength and weakness,—thine
own ways;
Whether to knock against the gates of Rome,
Or rudely visit them in parts remote,
To fright them, ere destroy. But come in:
Let me commend thee first to those that shall
Say yea to thy desires. A thousand welcomes!
And more a friend than e'er an enemy;

Yet, Marcius, that was much. Your hand: most
welcome!
Exeunt Coriolanus and Aufidius. The
two Servingmen come forward.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: Here's a strange alteration!

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: By my hand, I had thought to have strucken him with a cudgel: and yet my mind gave me his clothes made a false report of him.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: What an arm he has! he turned me about with his finger and his thumb, as one would set up a top.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: Nay, I knew by his face that there was something in him: he had, sir, a kind of face, methought,— I cannot tell how to term it.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: He had so; looking as it were —would I were hanged, but I thought there was more in him than I could think.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: So did I, I'll be sworn: he is simply the rarest man i' the world.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: I think he is: but a greater soldier than he you wot one.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: Serv. Who, my master?

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: Nay, it's no matter for that.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: Worth six on him.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: Nay, not so neither: but I take him to be the greater soldier.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: Serv. Faith, look you, one cannot tell how to say that: for the defence of a town, our general is excellent.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p:
Ay,and for an assault too.
Re-enter third Servingman.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: O slaves, I can tell you news. — news, you rascals!

sp.speaker: First and Sec. Serv.
sp.p: What, what, what? let's partake.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: I would not be a Roman, of all nations; I had as lieve be a condemned man.

sp.speaker: First and Sec. Serv.
sp.p: Wherefore? wherefore?

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: Why, here's he that was wont to thwack our general, Caius Marcius.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: Why do you say 'thwack our general'?

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: I do not say 'thwack our general;' but he was always good enough for him.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: Come, we are fellows and friends: he was ever too hard for him; I have heard him say so himself.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: He was too hard for him directly, to say the troth on 't: before Corioli he scotched him and notched him like a carbonado.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: An he had been cannibally given, he might have broiled and eaten him too.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: But, more of thy news?

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: Why, he is so made on here within, as if he were son and heir to Mars; set at upper end o' the table; no question asked him by any of the senators, but they stand bald before him: our general himself makes a mistress of him; sanctifies himself with's hand and turns up the whites o' the eye to his discourse. But the bottom of the news is, our general is cut i' the middle and but one half of what he was yesterday; for the other has half, by the entreaty and grant of the whole table. He'll go, he says, and sowl the porter of Rome gates by the ears: he will mow all down before him, and leave his passage polled.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: And he's as like to do 't as any man I can imagine.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: Do't! he will do't; for, look you, sir, he has as many friends as enemies; which friends, sir, as it were, durst not, look you, sir, show themselves, as we term it, his friends whilst he's in directitude.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: Directitude! what's that?

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: But when they shall see, sir, his crest up again, and the man in blood, they will out of their burrows, like conies after rain, and revel all with him.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: But when goes this forward?

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: To-morrow; to-day; presently; you shall have the drum struck up this afternoon: 'tis, as it were, a parcel of their feast, and to be executed ere they wipe their lips.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: Why, then we shall have a stirring world again. This peace is nothing, but to rust iron, increase tailors, and breed ballad-makers.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: Let me have war, say I; it exceeds peace as far as day does night; it's spritely, waking, audible, and full of vent. Peace is a very apoplexy, lethargy; mulled, deaf, sleepy, insensible; a getter of more bastard children than war's a destroyer of men.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: 'Tis so: and as war, in some sort, may be said to be a ravisher, so it cannot be denied but peace is a great maker of cuckolds.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: Ay, and it makes men hate one another.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.p: Reason; because they then less need one another. The wars for my money. I hope to see Romans as cheap as Volscians. They are rising, they are rising.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: In, in, in, in! Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l:
We hear not of him, neither need we fear
him;
His remedies are tame i' the present peace
And quietness of the people, which before
Were in wild hurry. Here do we make his friends
Blush that the world goes well, who rather had,
Though they themselves did suffer by 't, behold
Dissentious numbers pestering streets than see
Our tradesmen singing in their shops and going
About their functions friendly.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l:
We stood to 't in good time.
EnterMenenius. Is this Menenius?

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l:
'Tis he, 'tis he: O, he is grown most kind
of late.

sp.speaker: Both Tri.
sp.l: Hail, sir!

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Hail to you both!

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Your Coriolanus
Is not much miss'd, but with his friends:
The commonwealth doth stand, and so would do,
Were he more angry at it.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
All's well; and might have been much
better, if
He could have temporized.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Where is he, hear you?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
Nay, I hear nothing: his mother and
his wife

Hear nothing from him.
Enter three or four Citizens.

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l: The gods preserve you both!

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: God-den, our neighbours.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: God-den to you all, god-den to you all.

sp.speaker: First Cit.
sp.l:
Ourselves, our wives, our children,
on our knees,
Are bound to pray for you both.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Live, and thrive!

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l:
Farewell, kind neighbours: we wish'd
Coriolanus
Had loved you as we did.

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l: Now the gods keep you

sp.speaker: Both Tri.
sp.l:
Farewell, farewell.
Exeunt Citizens.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: This is a happier and more comely time
Than when these fellows ran about the streets,
Crying confusion.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Calus Marcus was
A worthy officer i' the war; but insolent,
O'ercome with pride, ambitious past all thinking,
Self-loving,—

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: And affecting one sole throne,
Without assistance.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: I think not so.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: We should by this, to all our lamentation,
If he had gone forth consul, found it so.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l:
The gods have well prevented it, and
Rome

Sits safe and still without him.
Enter an Ædile.

sp.speaker: Æd.
sp.l: Worthy tribunes,
There is a slave, whom we have put in prison,
Reports, the Volsces with two several powers
Are enter'd in the Roman territories,
And with the deepest malice of the war
Destroy what lies before 'em.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: 'Tis Aufidius,
Who, hearing of our Marcius' banishment,
Thrusts forth his horns again into the world;

Which were inshell'd when Marcius stood for
Rome,
And durst not once peep out.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Come, what talk you
Of Marcius?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l:
Go see this rumourer whipp'd. It
cannot be
The Volsces dare break with us.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Cannot be!
We have record that very well it can,
And three examples of the like have been
Within my age. But reason with the fellow,
Before you punish him, where he heard this,
Lest you shall chance to whip your information
And beat the messenger who bids beware
Of what is to be dreaded.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Tell not me:
I know this cannot be.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l:
Not possible.
Enter a Messenger.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.l:
The nobles in great earnestness are
going
All to the senate-house: some news is come
That turns their countenances.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: 'Tis this slave;—
Go whip him 'fore the people's eyes:—his raising;
Nothing but his report.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.l: Yes, worthy sir,
The slave's report is seconded; and more,
More fearful, is deliver'd.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: What more fearful?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.l: It is spoke freely out of many mouths—
How probable I do not know—that Marcius,
Join'd with Aufidius, leads a power 'gainst Rome,
And vows revenge as spacious as between
The young'st and oldest thing.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: This is most likely!

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l:
Raised only, that the weaker sort may
wish
Good Marcius home again.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: The very trick on 't.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: This is unlikely:
He and Aufidius can no more atone

Than violentest contrariety.
Enter a second Messenger.

sp.speaker: Sec. Mess.
sp.l: You are sent for to the senate:
A fearful army, led by Caius Marcius
Associated with Aufidius, rages
Upon our territories; and have already
O'erborne their way, consumed with fire, and took

What lay before them.
Enter COMINIUS.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: O, you have made good work?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: What news? what news?

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l:
You have holp to ravish your own
daughters and
To melt the city leads upon your pates,
To see your wives dishonour'd to your noses,—

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: What 's the news? what 's the news?

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Your temples burned in their cement, and
Your franchises, whereon you stood, confined
Into an auger's bore.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Pray now, your news?

You have made fair work, I fear me.—Pray, your
news?—
If Marcius should be join'd with Volscians,—

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: If!
He is their god: he leads them like a thing
Made by some other deity than nature,
That shapes men better; and they follow him,
Against us brats, with no less confidence
Than boys pursuing summer butterflies,
Or butchers killing flies.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: You have made good work,
You and your apron-men; you that stood so much
Upon the voice of occupation and
The breath of garlic-eaters!

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: He will shake
Your Rome about your ears.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: As Hercules

Did shake down mellow fruit. You have made
fair work!

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: But is this true, sir?

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Ay; and you'll look pale
Before you find it other. All the regions
Do smilingly revolt; and who resist
Are mock'd for valiant ignorance,

And perish constant fools. Who is't can blame
him?
Your enemies and his find something in him.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: We are undone, unless
The noble man have mercy.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Who shall ask it?
The tribunes cannot do't for shame; the people
Deserve such pity of him as the wolf
Does of the shepherds: for his best friends, if they

Should say 'Be good to Rome,' they charged him
even
As those should do that had deserved his hate
And therein show'd like enemies.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: 'Tis true:
If he were putting to my house the brand
That should consume it, I have not the face

To say 'Beseech you, cease.' You have made
fair hands,
You and your crafts! you have crafted fair!

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: You have brought
A trembling upon Rome, such as was never
So incapable of help.

sp.speaker: Both Tri.
sp.l: Say not we brought it.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
How! Was it we? we loved him; but,
like beasts
And cowardly nobles, gave way unto your clusters,
Who did hoot him out o' the city.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: But I fear
They'll roar him in again. Tullus Aufidius,
The second name of men, obeys his points
As if he were his officer: desperation
Is all the policy, strength and defence,

That Rome can make against them.
Enter a troop of Citizens.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Here come the clusters.
And is Aufidius with him? You are they
That made the air unwholesome, when you cast
Your stinking greasy caps in hooting at
Coriolanus' exile. Now he's coming;
And not a hair upon a soldier's head
Which will not prove a whip: as many coxcombs
As you threw caps up will he tumble down,
And pay you for your voices. 'Tis no matter;
If he could burn us all into one coal,
We have deserved it.

sp.speaker: Citizens.
sp.l: Faith, we hear fearful news.

sp.speaker: First Cit.
sp.l: For mine own part,
When I said, banish him, I said, 'twas pity.

sp.speaker: Sec. Cit.
sp.p: And so did I.

sp.speaker: Third Cit.
sp.p: And so did I; and, to say the truth, so did very many of us: that we did, we did for the best; and though we willingly consented to his banishment, yet it was against our will.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Ye're goodly things, you voices!

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: You have made

Good work, you and your cry Shall's to the
Capitol ?

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l:
O, ay, what else?
Exeunt Cominius and Menenius.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l:
Go, masters, get you home; be not
dismay'd:
These are a side that would be glad to have
This true which they so seem to fear. Go home,
And show no sign of fear.

sp.speaker: First Cit.
sp.p: The gods be good to us! Come, masters, let's home. I ever said we were i' the wrong when we banished him.

sp.speaker: Sec. Cit.
sp.p:
So did we all. But, come, let's home.
Exeunt Citizens.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: I do not like this news.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Nor I.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l:
Let's to the Capitol. Would half my
wealth
Would buy this for a lie!

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Pray, let us go. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE VII
div.stage:
A camp, at a small distance
from Rome.

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: Do they still fly to the Roman?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l:
I do not know what witchcraft's in him,
but
Your soldiers use him as the grace 'fore meat,
Their talk at table, and their thanks at end;
And you are darken'd in this action, sir,
Even by your own.

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: I cannot help it now,
Unless, by using means, I lame the foot
Of our design. He bears himself more proudlier,
Even to my person, than I thought he would
When first I did embrace him: yet his nature
In that's no changeling; and I must excuse
What cannot be amended.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Yet I wish, sir—
I mean for your particular,—you had not
Join'd in commission with him; but either
Had borne the action of yourself, or else
To him had left it solely.

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: I understand thee well; and be thou sure,
When he shall come to his account, he knows not
What I can urge against him. Although it seems,
And so he thinks, and is no less apparent
To the vulgar eye, that he bears all things fairly,

And shows good husbandry for the Volscian
state,
Fights dragon-like, and does achieve as soon
As draw his sword; yet he hath left undone
That which shall break his neck or hazard mine,
Whene'er we come to our account.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l:
Sir, I beseech you, think you he'll carry
Rome?

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: All places yield to him ere he sits down;
And the nobility of Rome are his:
The senators and patricians love him too:
The tribunes are no soldiers; and their people
Will be as rash in the repeal, as hasty
To expel him thence. I think he'll be to Rome
As is the osprey to the fish, who takes it
By sovereignty of nature. First he was
A noble servant to them; but he could not
Carry his honours even: whether 'twas pride,
Which out of daily fortune ever taints
The happy man; whether defect of judgement,
To fail in the disposing of those chances
Which he was lord of; or whether nature,
Not to be other than one thing, not moving

From the casque to the cushion, but commanding
peace
Even with the same austerity and garb
As he controll'd the war; but one of these—
As he hath spices of them all, not all,
For I dare so far free him—made him fear'd,
So hated, and so banish'd: but he has a merit,
To choke it in the utterance. So our virtues
Lie in the interpretation of the time:
And power, unto itself most commendable,
Hath not a tomb so evident as a chair
To extol what it hath done.
One fire drives out one fire; one nail, one nail;

Rights by rights falter, strengths by strengths do
fail.
Come, let's away. When, Caius, Rome is thine,
Thou art poor'st of all; then shortly art thou mine. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE I
div.stage:
Enter MENENIUS, COMINIUS, SICINUS, BRUTUS,
and others.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
No, I'll not go: you hear what he hath
said
Which was sometime his general; who loved him
In a most dear particular. He call'd me father:
But what o' that? Go, you that banish'd him;
A mile before his tent fall down, and knee
The way into his mercy: nay, if he coy'd
To hear Cominous speak, I'll keep at home.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: He would not seem to know me.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Do you hear?

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Yet one time did he call me by my name:
I urged our old acquaintance, and the drops
That we have bled together. Coriolanus
He would not answer to; forbad all names;
He was a kind of nothing, titleless,
Till he had forged himself a name o' the fire
Of burning Rome.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Why, so: you have made good work!
A pair of tribunes that have rack'd for Rome,
To make coals cheap,—a noble memory!

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: I minded him how royal 'twas to pardon
When it was less expected: he replied,
It was a bare petition of a state
To one whom they had punish'd.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Very well:
Could he say less?

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: I offer'd to awaken his regard
For 's private friends: his answer to me was,
He could not stay to pick them in a pile
Of noisome musty chaff: he said 'twas folly,
For one poor grain or two, to leave unburnt,
And still to nose the offence.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: For one poor grain or two!
I am one of those; his mother, wife, his child,
And this brave fellow too, we are the grains:
You are the musty chaff; and you are smelt
Above the moon: we must be burnt for you.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l:
Nay, pray, be patient: if you refuse your
aid
In this so never-needed help, yet do not
Upbraid's with our distress. But, sure, if you

Would be your country's pleader, your good
tongue,
More than the instant army we can make,
Might stop our countryman.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: No, I'll not meddle.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Pray you, go to him.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: What should I do?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Only make trial what your love can do
For Rome, towards Marcius.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Well, and say that Marcius
Return me, as Cominius is return'd,
Unheard; what then?
But as a discontented friend, grief-shot
With his unkindness? say't be so?

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Yet your good will

Must have that thanks from Rome, after the
measure
As you intended well.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: I'll undertake 't:
I think he'll hear me. Yet, to bite his lip
And hum at good Cominius, much unhearts me.
He was not taken well; he had not dined:
The veins unfill'd, our blood is cold, and then
We pout upon the morning, are unapt
To give or to forgive; but when we have stuff'd

These pipes and these conveyances of our
blood
With wine and feeding, we have suppler souls

Than in our priest-like fasts: therefore I'll watch
him
Till he be dieted to my request,
And then I'll set upon him.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l:
You know the very road into his
kindness,
And cannot lose your way.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Good faith, I'll prove him, 60

Speed how it will. I shall ere long have
knowledge
Of my success. Exit.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: He'll never hear him.

sp.speaker: Sic.
sp.l: Not?

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: I tell you, he does sit in gold, his eye
Red as 'twould burn Rome; and his injury
The gaoler to his pity. I kneel'd before him;
'Twas very faintly he said 'Rise;' dismiss'd me
Thus, with his speechless hand; what he would do,
He sent in writing after me; what he would not,
Bound with an oath to yield to his conditions:
So that all hope is vain,
Unless his noble mother, and his wife;
Who, as I hear, mean to solicit him
For mercy to his country. Therefore, let's hence,
And with our fair entreaties haste them on. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE II
div.stage:
Entrance of the Volscian camp
before Rome. Two Sentinels on guard.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.l: Stay: whence are you?

sp.speaker: Sec. Sen.
sp.l: Stand, and go back.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l:
You guard like men; 'tis well: but, by
your leave,
I am an officer of state, and come
To speak with Coriolanus.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.l: From whence?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: From Rome.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.l:
You may not pass, you must
return: our general
Will no more hear from thence.

sp.speaker: Sec. Sen.
sp.l:
You'll see your Rome embraced
with fire before
You'll speak with Coriolanus.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Good my friends,
If you have heard your general talk of Rome,
And of his friends there, it is lots to blanks,
My name hath touch'd your ears: it is Menenius.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.l:
Be it so; go back: the virtue of
your name
Is not here passable.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: I tell thee, fellow,
Thy general is my lover: I have been
The book of his good acts, whence men have read
His fame unparallel'd, haply amplified;
For I have ever verified my friends,
Of whom he's chief, with all the size that verity
Would without lapsing suffer: nay, sometimes,
Like to a bowl upon a subtle ground,
I have tumbled past the throw; and in his praise

Have almost stamp'd the leasing: therefore,
fellow,
I must have leave to pass.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.p: Faith, sir, if you had told as many lies in his behalf as you have uttered words in your own, you should not pass here; no, though it were as virtuous to lie as to live chastely. Therefore, go back.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Prithee, fellow, remember my name is Menenius, always factionary on the party of your general.

sp.speaker: Sec. Sen.
sp.p: Howsoever you have been his liar, as you say you have, I am one that, telling true under him, must say, you cannot pass. Therefore, go back.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Hath he dined, canst thou tell? for
I would not speak with him till after dinner.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.p: You are a Roman, are you?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: I am, as thy general is.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.p: Then you should hate Rome, as he does. Can you, when you have pushed out your gates the very defender of them, and, in a violent popular ignorance, given your enemy your shield, think to front his revenges with the easy groans of old women, the virginal palms of your daughters, or with the palsied intercession of such a decayed dotant as you seem to be? Can you think to blow out the intended fire your city is ready to flame in, with such weak breath as this? No, you are deceived; therefore, back to Rome, and prepare for your execution: you are condemned, our general has sworn you out of reprieve and pardon.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Sirrah, if thy captain knew I were here, he would use me with estimation.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.p: Come, my captain knows you not.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: I mean, thy general.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.p: My general cares not for you. Back, I say, go; lest I let forth your half-pint of blood; back,—that's the utmost of your having: back.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p:
Nay, but, fellow, fellow—
Enter CORIOLANUS and AUFIDIUS.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Now, you companion, I'll say an errand for you: you shall know now that I am in estimation; you shall perceive that a Jack guardant cannot office me from my son Coriolanus: guess, but by my entertainment with him, if thou standest not i' the state of hanging, or of some death more long in spectatorship, and crueller in suffering; behold now presently, and swoon for what's to come upon thee. [To Cor.] The glorious gods sit in hourly synod about thy particular prosperity, and love thee no worse than thy old father Menenius does! O my son, my son! thou art preparing fire for us; look thee, here's water to quench it. I was hardly moved to come to thee; but being assured none but myself could move thee, I have been blown out of your gates with sighs; and conjure thee to pardon Rome, and thy petitionary countrymen. The good gods assuage thy wrath, and turn the dregs of it upon this varlet here,—this, who, like a block, hath denied my access to thee.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Away!

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: How! away!

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
Wife, mother, child, I know not. My
affairs
Are servanted to others: though I owe
My revenge properly, my remission lies
In Volscian breasts. That we have been familiar,
Ingrate forgetfulness shall poison, rather
Than pity note how much. Therefore, be gone.
Mine ears against your suits are stronger than

Your gates against my force. Yet, for I loved
thee,

Take this along; I writ it for thy sake,
Gives a letter.
And would have sent it. Another word, Menenius,
I will not hear thee speak. This man, Aufidius,
Was my beloved in Rome: yet thou behold'st!

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l:
You keep a constant temper.
Exeunt Coriolanus and Aufidius.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.l: Now, sir, is your name Menenius ?

sp.speaker: Sec. Sen.
sp.p: 'Tis a spell, you see, of much power: you know the way home again.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.p: Do you hear how we are shent for keeping your greatness back?

sp.speaker: Sec. Sen.
sp.p: What cause, do you think, I have to swoon?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: I neither care for the world nor your general: for such things as you, I can scarce think there's any, ye're so slight. He that hath a will to die by himself fears it not from another: let your general do his worst. For you, be that you are, long; and your misery increase with your age! I say to you, as I was said to, Away! Exit.

sp.speaker: First Sen.
sp.p: A noble fellow, I warrant him.

sp.speaker: Sec. Sen.
sp.p: The worthy fellow is our gen eral: he's a rock, the oak not to be wind-shaken. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
We will before the walls of Rome
to-morrow
Set down our host. My partner in this action,

You must report to the Volscian lords, how
plainly
I have borne this business.

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: Only their ends
You have respected: stopp'd your ears against
The general suit of Rome; never admitted
A private whisper, no, not with such friends
That thought them sure of you.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: This last old man,
Whom with a crack'd heart I have sent to Rome,
Loved me above the measure of a father;
Nay, godded me, indeed. Their latest refuge
Was to send him; for whose old love I have,

Though I show'd sourly to him, once more
offer'd
The first conditions, which they did refuse
And cannot now accept; to grace him only
That thought he could do more, a very little
I have yielded to: fresh embassies and suits,
Nor from the state nor private friends, hereafter

Will I lend ear to. Ha! what shout is this?
Shout within.
Shall I be tempted to infringe my vow

In the same time 'tis made? I will not.
Enter, in mourning habits, VIRGILIA,
VOLUMNIA, leading young MARCIUS, VALERIA,
and Attendants.

My wife comes foremost; then the honour'd
